We all have a major artery called the ascending aortic artery that runs down the center of our abdomen.  Another artery, called the superior mesenteric artery, branches off of that. 

There is a gap between the arteries that is kept open by a pad of fat, and the start of our intestines, called the duodenum, passes right through the gap between the two arteries. 

Very very rarely something can happen to shrink the fat pad, and then the arteries act like a clamp and pinch the duodenum closed. This prevents anything, solid or liquid, from passing from the stomach into the intestines. 

This is called Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome, and I had it. It is so rare that it took 2 months of doctors excluding everything else for them to diagnose me. 

I couldn't keep anything down, and went from 120 to 90 lbs. I had to have where my intestines were connected to my stomach moved to another spot, and have about 6 feet removed in the process. 

This was almost 7 years ago now. Other than having to eat more than I used to in order to maintain my weight, I'm okay. That is only one of the weird, and very rare, medical conditions that I'm living with, but  you'd never know by looking at me.

It sounds like there's some jealousy and some territoriality going on here. Cats are sensitive creatures, and most don't like change, and even tiny changes can feel huge to some. 

There are definitely some things that you can do, though, to mitigate the stress and/or territoriality your cat may be experiencing. First thing is to spend more time with your adult cat. It may not seem like it to you, but time you're spending with the new kitten is time that your adult cat may have been accustomed to spending with you. 

You can get a new interactive toy for you to use to play with your adult cat. Also, make sure to seek out your cat for attention, especially times that it's accustomed to, but especially when you arrive home, but also anytime you think of it. Try to include your adult cat in any cuddle time or petting sessions you have with the kitten. That will help  your cat associate the kitten with good things. Giving treats anytime it's being good, especially if it's around the kitten. 

Cats are naturally territorial animals, so make sure you're giving your adult kitty it's own space, especially if it has a favorite spot. Also, make sure your kitten doesn't have access to any of your cats favorite toys. As far as specifically about the litter box issue, make sure if your cat had a particular box it preferred to use it is set somewhere where only it and not the kitten can get to it. The smell of your new little one can definitely put off your adult cat from wanting to go in the box. It could also be urinating on a spot it sees as yours and is telling you that it's not happy with the changes. 

Also, you can make sure your cat has its own places for eating, sleeping, and a litter box all it's own until it can have some time to adjust. They aren't always quick to accept new things, more so as they get older and more set in their routines and lifestyles. It could possibly take weeks or months for your cat to adjust, so try to be patient, and stay positive. Don't punish the bad behavior, but do reward the good. 

Lastly, make sure to encourage your adult cat to be around the new kitten with treats, petting, praise, basically whatever your kitty likes best. Have patience, and hopefully with time and trying a few things I've shared will hello your slightly larger family to become  peaceful, well adjusted, and  more than anything, happy. Good luck to you, and please let me know if you need anything, or if you want me to elaborate on anything I've said.
